ambitious.meaning: having a strong desire to succeed or achieve something
ambitious.example: She is ambitious and wants to run her own company one day.

rebellious.meaning: unwilling to obey rules or accept normal standards of behaviour
rebellious.example: As a teenager he was rebellious and often argued with his parents.

adventurous.meaning: willing to take risks and try new experiences
adventurous.example: They are adventurous travellers who prefer remote destinations.

argumentative.meaning: often disagreeing or starting arguments with other people
argumentative.example: He becomes argumentative when he is tired.

stubborn.meaning: determined not to change your mind or attitude
stubborn.example: She is too stubborn to admit she made a mistake.

curious.meaning: interested in learning about new things
curious.example: Young children are naturally curious about the world around them.

cheerful.example: Despite the bad news she remained cheerful.

sociable.meaning: enjoying the company of other people
sociable.example: He is very sociable and makes friends easily.

outgoing.meaning: friendly and enjoying meeting new people
outgoing.example: Her outgoing personality helps her in sales.

reliable.meaning: able to be trusted or depended on
reliable.example: She is a reliable colleague who always meets deadlines.

optimistic.example: He remains optimistic about the project’s success.

pessimistic.example: She has a pessimistic view of the economy.

realistic.meaning: accepting situations as they really are
realistic.example: We need a realistic plan that we can actually achieve.

generous.meaning: willing to give money, time or help freely
generous.example: It was generous of them to pay for everyone’s meal.

thoughtful.meaning: showing care and consideration for others
thoughtful.example: He wrote a thoughtful note to thank her.

practical.meaning: relating to real situations rather than ideas
practical.example: She gave me some practical advice about moving house.

musical.meaning: having a natural ability or interest in music
musical.example: Both children are very musical and play several instruments.

experienced.meaning: having knowledge or skill from doing something for a long time
experienced.example: We need an experienced teacher for this advanced class.

contribute.meaning: to help to cause or increase something
contribute.example: Regular exercise can contribute to better health.

inherit.meaning: to receive characteristics or property from parents or family
inherit.example: She inherited her mother’s artistic talent.

influence.meaning: to have an effect on the way someone thinks or behaves
influence.example: His teachers strongly influenced his choice of career.

immigrant.meaning: a person who comes to live permanently in a foreign country
immigrant.example: Many immigrants face challenges when settling in a new country.

identity.meaning: the qualities that make a person different from others
identity.example: Moving abroad made her question her cultural identity.

lifestyle.meaning: the way in which a person lives
lifestyle.example: A healthy lifestyle includes good food and regular exercise.

achievement.meaning: something that has been done successfully
achievement.example: Winning the award was a great achievement for the team.

disappointment.meaning: the feeling of being sad because something did not happen as expected
disappointment.example: Failing the exam was a huge disappointment.

interact.meaning: to communicate or work together with someone
interact.example: Children learn by interacting with their peers.

co-founded.meaning: to start an organisation together with someone else
co-founded.example: She co-founded the design studio with two friends.

adventurous.meaning: willing to take risks and try new experiences
adventurous.example: An adventurous spirit led them to explore the mountains.

talented.meaning: having a natural ability to do something well
talented.example: She is a talented designer with original ideas.

helpful.example: The staff were very helpful when we had a problem.

hopeful.example: We are hopeful that the situation will improve.

likeable.example: He has a likeable personality that puts people at ease.

artistic.meaning: showing skill or imagination in art
artistic.example: She has an artistic eye for colour and composition.

emotional.example: The film had a very emotional ending.

sociable.meaning: enjoying spending time with other people
sociable.example: Warm climates are said to make people more sociable.

blocks.instruction: Read the article. Does it include any of your ideas?

cards.text: Our experiences have a huge impact on our personalities. The jobs we do, the people we meet, our achievements and disappointments all contribute to the kind of person we are. What other factors might also be important?

A lot of people think that our personality is shaped by the size of our family and our position in it. Some argue that first-born children are more likely to be ambitious achievers. Younger children, on the other hand, might be more rebellious and willing to break rules. The youngest child of a family is often fun-loving and adventurous – always keen to try new things. We can inherit personality characteristics, too, like being argumentative or stubborn.

Research suggests that the language we speak influences our personality and the way we think. In a recent survey of international students, Gosia, a Polish-born immigrant in the USA, says that when she speaks English, she feels ‘more curious about the world’. Natasha, who speaks several languages, says that she feels more romantic when she’s speaking in Portuguese, more cheerful and likely to smile when speaking Italian and more relaxed when speaking in Greek.

Other studies show that where we live or were born might also influence our lifestyle, our personality and the way that we interact with others socially. People living in warmer climates often see themselves as more sociable and outgoing, whilst people from mountainous areas seem to be more open to new experiences.

blocks.instruction: Read the blog post. What do you learn about Sydney’s family background, personality and attitude to work?

cards.text: My name is Sydney and I was born in Sacramento, in the USA. My parents are immigrants from China, so I’ve grown up speaking Mandarin at home but English at school and with my friends. We have family in China so we have always visited regularly. As well as my U.S. identity, I would say that I identify quite strongly with my Asian roots.

In my personal life, I would like to think that I’m quite adventurous. I love trying out new experiences. I’m not particularly good at either, but I’m quite stubborn, so I plan to keep going. I’m also outgoing and sociable.

In my work, I’m very ambitious. I never settle for anything less than the best and always work hard. In terms of my experience, I’ve been designing websites for over seven years. I co-founded WebDesignSY, an award-winning creative studio. I’ve designed websites for businesses, charities and individuals. I’ve also taught several courses in design at the California Institute of Arts and Technology. I love nothing more than thinking of interesting ways to represent you and your brand, so please get in touch.

sections.title: Grammar Bank – present perfect simple and continuous

rules.label: Overview
rules.rule: We use both the present perfect simple and the present perfect continuous to talk about situations or actions which started in the past and continue into the present. Sometimes there is no important difference between the two tenses, particularly with verbs such as work, live and study.
rules.example: Mauro has lived/has been living in Bologna since 2010.

rules.label: Focusing on the result of the activity
rules.rule: We use the present perfect simple to focus on the result of a completed activity.
rules.example: He’s passed all of his exams. (Focuses on the result – passing the exams)

rules.label: Focusing on the activity itself
rules.rule: We use the present perfect continuous to focus on the activity itself.
rules.example: He’s been studying for his exams. (Focuses on the activity of studying)

rules.label: How many? vs. How long?
rules.rule: We use the present perfect simple to answer the questions: ‘How many?’, ‘How much?’ or ‘How far?’ We use the present perfect continuous to answer the question: ‘How long?’ and to emphasise that an action has continued for a long time (using for and since to describe the duration), or is repeated. We often use the present perfect continuous with verbs that describe long actions, such as wait, stay, play, sit, stand, write, etc.
rules.example: We’ve interviewed more than 100 applicants (How many?) We’ve raised £1,000 for charity. (How much?) They’ve driven over 3,000 kilometres. (How far?) We’ve been waiting for over forty minutes now! He’s been sitting on that bench since this morning.

rules.label: Completed vs. unfinished actions
rules.rule: We use the present perfect simple to describe completed actions. We use the present perfect continuous to describe actions that are unfinished or in progress.
rules.example: Oh no, I’ve missed the bus! (The bus has gone, so the action is completed.) I’m afraid she’s left the office. (She isn’t here now, so the action is completed.) I’ve been learning Mandarin. (I’m still learning, so the action is not completed.) She’s been trying to speak to you. (She still hasn’t spoken to you, so she’s still trying.)

rules.label: State verbs, experiences and habits
rules.rule: We use the present perfect simple, NOT the present perfect continuous, with state verbs, to talk about states or situations that started in the past and are in progress. We also use the present perfect simple with the words always, ever and never to talk about experiences and habits.
rules.example: How long have you known Jessica? I’ve owned this car since 2009. He’s never driven to work, he always goes by bike. I’ve always baked my own bread.
